finding: NIH-funded research contributed to every new molecular entity approved by FDA 2010-2016
citation: Cleary EG, Beierlein JM, Khanuja NS, McNamee LM, Ledley FD (2018) PNAS 115(10):2329-2334
notes: Contribution was mostly basic research on drug targets, not the drugs themselves. 'Contributed' is broad: any linked NIH-funded publication.

finding: NIH project costs linked to those 210 drugs, 2000-2016

finding: First-in-class drugs among the 210 and NIH funding linked to them
citation: Cleary et al. (2018) PNAS (PMC summary)

finding: FDA-approved drugs, vaccines or new indications discovered in public-sector research institutions over 40 years
citation: Stevens AJ et al. (2011) NEJM 364(6) 'The role of public-sector research in the discovery of drugs and vaccines'
notes: Abstract says 40 years; a press release said 30 years. 93 small molecules, 36 biologics, 15 vaccines.

finding: Public-sector-discovered drugs received FDA Priority Review at twice the rate of all approvals
citation: Stevens et al. (2011) NEJM, as reported by ScienceDaily press release
notes: Press release wording, not the abstract.

finding: Drugs with a public-sector patent (direct public role), drugs approved 1988-2005
citation: Sampat BN, Lichtenberg FR (2011) Health Affairs 30(2):332-339

finding: Government funding played an indirect role (basic research cited by drug patents)
value: ~50 of all drugs; ~67 of priority-review drugs
citation: Sampat & Lichtenberg (2011) Health Affairs
notes: Abstract says 'almost half' and 'almost two-thirds'.

finding: US patents that rely on federally funded research (directly or via cited papers/patents), 1926-2017
citation: Fleming L, Greene H, Li G, Marx M, Yao D (2019) Science 364(6446):1139-1141
notes: Read in university press release, not the paper. Authors call it conservative; share rising over 90 years.

finding: Patents in chemistry and metallurgy relying on federally supported research
citation: Fleming et al. (2019) Science (press release)

finding: US basic research funded by federal government vs business, 2022

notes: 2022 values are estimates.

finding: US R&D funded by business, 2022
citation: NCSES (NSF 24-332)
notes: $570bn is in the text; the 76% share was computed by the fetch tool from a constant-dollar table. Treat as approximate.

finding: OECD gross R&D (GERD) and business R&D (BERD), 2023
citation: Scottish Government, GERD Scotland 2023, using OECD MSTI
notes: 74% is the ratio 1.99/2.70 (computed); an OECD release says 74% too but its page returned 403.

finding: Claim that every technology making the iPhone 'smart' (Internet, GPS, touch-screen, Siri) was government funded
citation: Mazzucato M, The Entrepreneurial State (publisher description)
notes: Publisher blurb, not peer reviewed. Contested by critics (e.g. nintil.com), not fetched. Funding the components is not the same as making the product.

finding: US public investment in mRNA covid-19 vaccines, 1985 to March 2022; of which before the pandemic
citation: Lalani HS et al. (2023) BMJ 380:e073747
notes: 92% ($29.2bn) of the total was vaccine purchases; 7% trials. Pre-pandemic: NIH $116m (35%), BARDA $148m (44%), DoD $72m (21%). A news summary said DoD $77m.

finding: ARPANET began as a DARPA-funded four-node network in 1969; the switch to TCP/IP in January 1983 marks the Internet
citation: DARPA, 'ARPANET' feature
notes: Official agency history (self-reported).

finding: GPS is a US-owned utility operated by the US Space Force; civilian service free worldwide
citation: GPS.gov (US government)

finding: World Wide Web proposed at CERN by Berners-Lee (March 1989); CERN put it in the public domain on 30 April 1993
citation: CERN Web@30 history
notes: A public lab giving away a key invention with no patent.

finding: WWII public R&D (OSRD) created US technology clusters with effects lasting to at least the 1970s and shifted US innovation toward funded fields
citation: Gross DP, Sampat BN (2023) AER 113(12):3323-3356 (NBER w27375)
notes: Mission-oriented public R&D under wartime urgency.

finding: Nobel Prize 2023 to Karikó and Weissman for nucleoside base modifications enabling mRNA vaccines; work was NIH-supported
citation: Nobel Assembly / NIH Record
notes: Pages returned 403; seen only in search snippets. Do not cite amounts.

finding: Extra private-sector patents per extra USD 10 million of NIH funding
citation: Azoulay P, Graff Zivin J, Li D, Sampat BN (2019) Review of Economic Studies 86(1):117-152
notes: Working paper version said 2.3 (abstract) / 3.1 (digest). Uses peer-review rules for causal identification.

finding: Private R&D added by a 10% rise in government-financed (defence) R&D: crowding in, not out
citation: Moretti E, Steinwender C, Van Reenen J (2025) Review of Economics and Statistics 107(1):14-27
notes: Induced private R&D raised productivity. A CEPR version said 4.3%.

finding: Social returns to innovation effort are 'many multiples of the investment costs' even under conservative assumptions
citation: Jones BF, Summers LH (2020) NBER w27863
notes: Abstract gives no single number.

finding: Markets under-provide innovation; short run: R&D tax credits and direct public funding most productive; long run: more human capital (STEM, immigration)
citation: Bloom N, Van Reenen J, Williams H (2019) JEP 33(3):163-184

finding: Nineteenth-century world's fairs (close to 15,000 innovations): countries without patent laws still innovated, but in a narrow set of industries where patents mattered less
notes: Patents shape the direction more than the level of innovation (level result stated in NBER WP version, seen in search only).

finding: Celera's temporary IP on genes reduced later research and product development
citation: Williams H (2013) Journal of Political Economy 121(1):1-27
notes: IP was contract-based, up to 2 years.

finding: Gene patents had no quantitatively important effect on follow-on innovation on average
citation: Sampat B, Williams H (2019) AER 109(1):203-236 (NBER w21666)
notes: Counterweight to Williams 2013: patents per se did not block; Celera's restrictive access did.

finding: Opening access to genetically engineered mice (NIH agreements) increased follow-on research, mainly via more diverse research paths
citation: Murray F, Aghion P, Dewatripont M, Kolev J, Stern S (2016) AEJ: Economic Policy 8(1) (NBER w14819)

finding: Royal Agricultural Society of England prizes 1839-1939 (worth over GBP 1 million today) strongly raised contest entries, especially the gold medal, and raised patent quality
citation: Brunt L, Lerner J, Nicholas T (2012) Journal of Industrial Economics 60(4):657-696 (CEPR DP6917)
notes: Prestige medals were especially effective: recognition, not just cash.

finding: Advance Market Commitment pilot for pneumococcal vaccine: donor commitment; result 3 vaccines, >150 million children immunised, ~700,000 lives saved (estimate)
citation: Kremer M, Levin J, Snyder CM (2020) AEA Papers and Proceedings 110:269-273
notes: Lives saved is the authors' estimate. A pull mechanism for a defined product.

finding: Ansari XPRIZE purse vs R&D spent by competing teams
citation: XPRIZE Foundation
notes: Self-reported by the prize organiser; leverage about 10x.

finding: Longitude prize: Board paid Harrison GBP 500 in 1737; in 1765 recommended GBP 10,000 for H4 with a second 10,000 conditional; Harrison said the Commissioners changed the rules
citation: Royal Museums Greenwich
notes: Lesson: prize rules must be fixed in advance and judged independently.

finding: Inducement prizes used for centuries; rigorous empirical evaluation needed to guide design
citation: Williams H (2012) Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 31(3):752-776

finding: Patent buyouts: government buys patents at auction-estimated value times a markup and puts them in the public domain
notes: Seen only in search summaries. Theoretical; no large-scale test.

finding: Supply-side value of widely used open source software (cost to rebuild once)

notes: Read in a blog quoting the abstract and an HBS institute page; HBS and SSRN pages returned 403.

finding: Demand-side value of OSS (cost if each firm rebuilt what it uses)
citation: Hoffmann, Nagle, Zhou (2024) HBS WP 24-038
notes: Estimate method contested (critics say firms would not rebuild everything).

finding: Firms would spend this many times more on software without OSS
citation: Hoffmann, Nagle, Zhou (2024)

finding: Share of OSS demand-side value generated by 5% of programmers
citation: Hoffmann, Nagle, Zhou (2024), as reported by HBS Digital Data Design Institute
notes: Value is highly concentrated in a few contributors; many OSS core developers are paid by firms (not quantified here).

finding: English Wikipedia: 7,258,752 articles (Nov 2026); >1,100,000 volunteers have edited >10 times; >30,000 make >5 edits/month
citation: Wikipedia, 'English Wikipedia'
notes: Tertiary source. Active editors peaked ~50,000 (2007) and fell to ~30,000 (2014): volunteer effort is real but not self-sustaining growth.

finding: Enjoyment-based intrinsic motivation (feeling creative) is the strongest driver of open source contribution
citation: Lakhani KR, Wolf RG (2005) in Perspectives on Free and Open Source Software, MIT Press
notes: SSRN returned 403; seen only in search snippet. Sample size (684) not verified.

finding: Meta-analysis of 128 experiments: engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation
citation: Deci EL, Koestner R, Ryan RM (1999) Psychological Bulletin 125(6):627-668
notes: All tangible and expected rewards also undermined it (no single d in abstract). Positive feedback enhanced it (d=0.33). Effects larger for children. Contested by Cameron & Pierce.

finding: Meta-analysis (k=183, N=212,468): intrinsic motivation predicts performance with or without incentives; it predicts quality better, incentives predict quantity better
citation: Cerasoli CP, Nicklin JM, Ford MT (2014) Psychological Bulletin 140(4):980-1008
notes: Directly performance-tied incentives weakened the role of intrinsic motivation.

finding: Paying a small amount produced worse performance than paying nothing; larger pay improved performance among paid groups
citation: Gneezy U, Rustichini A (2000) QJE 115(3):791-810
notes: 'Pay enough or don't pay at all'.

finding: Motivation crowding is empirically relevant and can in some cases dominate the price effect of incentives
citation: Frey BS, Jegen R (2001) Journal of Economic Surveys 15(5):589-611
notes: Survey of field, lab and circumstantial evidence.

finding: Switch from hourly pay to piece rates at Safelite raised output per worker
notes: About half incentive effect, half sorting of workers (per summaries). Simple measurable task.

finding: Rewards for approved employee ideas raised idea quality; no motivational crowding out; participation stayed higher after rewards ended
citation: Gibbs M, Neckermann S, Siemroth C (2014) ZEW DP 14-096; Review of Economics and Statistics 2017
notes: Randomised field experiment in a technology firm.

finding: Scientists funded with tolerance for early failure and long horizons (HHMI) produced high-impact papers at a much higher rate than similar NIH grantees and explored newer topics
citation: Azoulay P, Graff Zivin J, Manso G (2011) RAND Journal of Economics 42(3):527-554 (NBER w15466)
notes: Abstract gives no number.

finding: Lab experiment: tolerance for early failure plus reward for long-term success produced more exploration and discovery than fixed wage or standard pay-for-performance; threat of termination undermined innovation
citation: Ederer F, Manso G (2013) Management Science 59(7):1496-1513

finding: Pay inequality among coworkers whose productivity is hard to observe cut output and attendance; no effect when higher pay clearly matched higher productivity
citation: Breza E, Kaur S, Shamdasani Y (2018) QJE 133(2):611-663
notes: Working paper reported -0.24 SD and -12%. Indian manufacturing, one month.

finding: Workers told their pay is below their unit's median report lower satisfaction and more job search; above-median workers unaffected; rank matters more than level
citation: Card D, Mas A, Moretti E, Saez E (2012) AER 102(6):2981-3003
notes: Relevant to publishing multipliers.

finding: Hazard of dissolution for worker-managed firms vs conventional firms in Uruguay
citation: Burdín G (2014) ILR Review 67(1):202-238 (IZA DP 7412)
notes: Figure from the IZA working-paper abstract; excludes microenterprises; controls for tax.

finding: French labour-managed firms are as productive or more productive than conventional firms in all industries studied, and grow as fast or faster
citation: Fakhfakh F, Pérotin V, Gago M (2012) ILR Review 65(4):847-879

finding: Meta-analysis of 43 studies: profit sharing, worker ownership and participation positively associated with productivity; stronger in labour-managed firms
citation: Doucouliagos C (1995) ILR Review 49(1):58-77
notes: Mandated codetermination negatively associated.

finding: Worker co-ops survive at least as long as other firms, have more stable jobs and much narrower executive pay gaps

finding: Mondragon 2023: sales EUR 11.05 billion; 240 businesses of which 81 co-operatives; 70,500 workers
citation: Co-operative News (thenews.coop) on Mondragon 2023 results

finding: French worker co-ops 2014-2018: share of worker-owners among workers raises innovation; share among owners lowers it; co-ops not inherently less innovative

finding: Soviet growth 1960-1989 was the worst in the world after controlling for investment and human capital; low capital-labour substitution made diminishing returns severe

citation: Ofer G, 'Economic Growth, Soviet', Encyclopedia of Russian History

finding: Soviet TFP contributed ~30% of growth only in the 1930s, then diminished and turned negative; investment >30% of GNP; defence ~15% of GNP absorbed technology
citation: Ofer G, Encyclopedia of Russian History
notes: Notes 'difficulties in creating indigenous technological innovations'.

finding: Ratchet principle: planners set future targets from current performance, so good performance is punished with harder targets
citation: Weitzman ML (1980) Bell Journal of Economics 11(1):302-308
notes: Term traced to Berliner (1957) per secondary source.

finding: Soviet reformer: profitability falls when enterprises master new products; the incentive system 'is a direct impediment to increasing product quality or mastering new products'

notes: Primary source; an insider's critique.

finding: Soft budget constraint: loss-making enterprises are reliably bailed out, so bad projects are not stopped and good ones not rewarded

finding: Soviet industry encouraged established products by established processes; innovation threatened plan fulfilment and bonuses

finding: UK four-day week pilot 2022: 61 firms (~2,900 staff); at least 56 continued, 18 permanently; revenue +1.4%; sick days -65%

finding: Output proportional to hours below a threshold, rising more slowly above it (WWI British munitions workers)

notes: IZA page refused connection; seen only in search. The '49 hours' threshold is from press, not verified.

finding: Randomised grant evaluation (2,130 evaluator-proposal pairs): evaluators systematically score highly novel proposals lower
citation: Boudreau KJ, Guinan EC, Lakhani KR, Riedl C (2016) Management Science 62(10):2765-2783

finding: Among 102,740 funded NIH grants scoring in the top 20th percentile, the score explained only ~1% of variance in productivity; authors suggest a modified lottery
